overview.intro: The grammar component carries 7 marks and takes two forms: gap filling built on tenses and clauses, and re-ordering or transformation of sentences, with seven questions to be attempted out of eight. The section rewards accuracy under a simple rule rather than knowledge of terminology, so this unit works through the decisions a reader actually makes — which tense the time marker demands, what each blank needs grammatically, how clauses fit together, and how a sentence is recast without changing its meaning.

facts.label: Format
facts.value: Seven questions to be attempted out of the eight given.

facts.label: Re-ordering / transformation
facts.value: Rearranging words into a sentence, or recasting one construction into another with the meaning intact.

learningOutcomes: Choose verb forms by time marker, aspect and sequence of tenses.
Identify what each blank requires: verb, connector, article, preposition or pronoun.
Fit subordinate clauses into sentences with correct connectives.
Re-order words into grammatical sentences and transform constructions without altering meaning.

blocks.text: Nearly every tense item can be solved by finding its anchor. Words such as since, for, always, by the time, yesterday, next year and usually tell you the time frame before you look at the options; the gap tells you the aspect. Present perfect appears with unfinished time — since, so far, recently — and links a past action to the present moment; simple past appears with finished time — yesterday, ago, last week; future perfect places completion before a future point, signalled by by the time or by next year. Where two events are sequenced in the past, the earlier one takes the past perfect and the later the simple past, so “when I arrived, the train had left” is fixed by order rather than preference.

rows: She has worked here for ten years
by the time / by next year
The work will have been finished by Monday

items: Find the time anchor first; only then choose the verb form.
Sequence of tenses decides past perfect versus simple past in narrated events.
Passive forms keep the tense of the active verb: was being written, will be finished.
In gap filling, check agreement with the subject before anything else.

learn.title: Clauses: connectors and what the blank needs

blocks.text: Clause items test whether you can see the shape of the sentence. Every gap demands a grammatical category: a finite verb for a main clause, a subordinator for a subordinate one, a relative pronoun for a defining clause, or a connector for a contrast or condition. Read the sentence as two parts joined at the gap and ask what work the second part does relative to the first — is it cause, condition, contrast, time, purpose or result? Because, although, if, unless, which, who and where each commit you to a different relationship, and the meaning of the pair fixes the connector.

Two habits prevent most errors. First, check whether the clause is defining or non-defining: a defining clause adds essential identification and takes no commas, while a non-defining clause adds extra information and does. Second, after choosing, reread the whole sentence aloud in your head — a connector that fits the meaning but leaves the second clause without a finite verb is wrong, and a connector that fits the grammar but reverses the logic is equally wrong. The answer must satisfy both halves.

Re-ordering gives you a jumble of words and expects a sentence. Begin with the clause you can complete unaided — subject and verb — then attach its objects, modifiers and finally its adverbials, which most often belong at the end or in the position the emphasis requires. Punctuation comes last and follows from structure: if your sentence ends up beginning with a subordinate clause, it takes a comma at the break. Reading the finished sentence once confirms both meaning and order.

Transformation asks you to recast a sentence into another construction while keeping its meaning intact — active into direct and indirect speech, affirmative into negative, one degree of comparison into another, or a conditional rewritten. The method is invariant-first: decide what must not change (the time reference, the actor, the polarity of the claim) and then rebuild the sentence around that constant. Errors come from changing two things at once, so recast one element at a time and verify the meaning after each.

items.text: “If it does not rain, the match will be played.” → “Unless it rains, the match will be played.”
items.note: The condition is preserved because unless already carries the negative, so adding another not would invert the meaning — polarity must be checked, not copied.

items.text: Active: “The committee has approved the plan.” → Passive: “The plan has been approved by the committee.”
items.note: The perfect tense is preserved by has been, and the object becomes the subject.

blocks.text: Seven of eight questions must be attempted, so accuracy matters more than coverage: attempting all eight risks one wrong answer cancelling one right one, while attempting seven well protects the arithmetic. The commonest losses are of a specific kind — subject–verb disagreement after a phrase that interrupts the subject, a connector chosen for meaning but leaving no finite verb, tense chosen from habit instead of from the time marker, and transformation that silently changes polarity.

Practice is best done as short daily sets followed by classification of the errors: if tense items fail, the cause is usually the time marker not being read; if transformation items fail, the cause is usually two changes made at once. Because this section is only 7 of 80 marks, it should be prepared to reliable accuracy rather than to depth: the aim is to make these marks automatic and to spend study time on the reading and literature sections where the returns are larger.

items: Read the time anchor before choosing a tense.
Every blank needs a category: verb, connector, pronoun, article or preposition.
Check agreement with the subject after choosing a verb form.
Transformation keeps one invariant: time, actor or polarity.
Attempt seven of eight deliberately; accuracy beats coverage here.
Finish the section quickly — the literature section carries more marks.

vocabulary.meaning: The form of a verb locating an action in time and aspect.
Whether an action is completed, ongoing or extending to a point.
A group of words with a subject and a finite verb.
A word such as because or although that introduces a subordinate clause.
The rule governing verb forms when events are narrated in order.

questions.prompt: In the CBSE Class XI grammar item, how many questions are to be attempted out of how many given?
questions.explanation: The curriculum specifies seven questions to be done out of the eight given, for 7 marks.

questions.prompt: “She ______ in this school since 2015.” The correct form is:
questions.explanation: The marker since requires a present perfect continuous, which carries an action from the past up to the present.

questions.prompt: “When I reached the station, the train ______.” The correct form is:
questions.explanation: The earlier of two past actions takes the past perfect, so the train’s departure precedes the arrival.

questions.prompt: Which sentence preserves the meaning of “The work will be finished by Monday” in the active voice?
options: The manager will finish the work by Monday
The manager finished the work by Monday
The work will have finished by Monday
The manager finishes the work by Monday
questions.answer: The manager will finish the work by Monday
questions.explanation: The transformation keeps both the future reference and the completion point marked by by Monday.

questions.prompt: The connector that introduces a clause of contrast is __________ .
questions.explanation: Although introduces a concession: the second clause runs against the expectation set by the first. (Though, though and whereas are also accepted.)

questions.prompt: A clause that adds extra, non-essential information and is set off by commas is a __________ clause.
questions.explanation: A defining clause identifies its noun and takes no commas; a non-defining clause adds information the sentence can do without.

questions.prompt: State four steps for choosing the correct tense in a gap-fill item.
questions.answer: Four steps are: find the time marker in the sentence, since or for, yesterday, by next year and so on, which fixes the time frame; decide the aspect the situation requires — completed, ongoing or extending to a point; check the subject for agreement with the verb form; and, where two events are narrated in the past, place the earlier one in the past perfect and the later in the simple past. Reading the sentence aloud after the choice to confirm the meaning is also accepted.
questions.explanation: Each step must be an action taken on the sentence, not a statement that tenses matter.

questions.prompt: Explain how to re-order a jumbled set of words into a sentence.
questions.answer: Begin by finding the clause you can complete without help: the subject and its finite verb, which gives the sentence its spine. Attach the objects and complements that the verb requires, then the modifiers — adjectives, adverbs and phrases — which must sit next to the word they qualify, and place the adverbials of time and place last unless the sentence opens with them for emphasis. Punctuation follows structure rather than guesswork: if the sentence begins with a subordinate clause, a comma marks the break after it. The final step is to reread the sentence to check that the meaning is complete, the order is natural and nothing has been duplicated, since jumbled sets frequently contain a word that belongs to two positions and only one of them is correct.
questions.explanation: The method must be ordered: core clause, complements, modifiers, adverbials, punctuation, verification.

questions.prompt: Describe the method for transforming a sentence without changing its meaning.
questions.answer: Transformation means recasting a sentence into another construction — active into passive, direct into indirect speech, affirmative into negative, one degree of comparison into another, or a conditional rewritten — while its meaning remains the same. The method begins by identifying the invariants: the time reference must not move, the actor or patient must not be reassigned, and the polarity of the claim must not flip unless polarity is precisely what is being changed. With the invariants stated, change one element at a time. In the active-to-passive conversion, the object becomes the subject, the verb takes the appropriate form of be plus the past participle, and the tense of the original verb is preserved — a perfect active becomes a perfect passive through has or have been, a continuous becomes is or was being — while the original subject may appear after the verb in a by-phrase or be dropped where it is indefinite. In direct-to-indirect speech, the reporting verb governs the backshift of tense, the pronouns shift their person in relation to the speaker, and time and place expressions change to their reported equivalents, each of which is a separate decision that must be verified separately. In comparatives, moving between degrees changes the structure without altering the comparison, provided the second term keeps its place in the relation. The verification step is indispensable: reread the transformed sentence against the original and ask three questions — same time, same actor, same polarity? Errors concentrate where two elements are changed in a single move, which is why the one-change-at-a-time discipline produces reliable results rather than occasional luck.
questions.explanation: Full marks need the invariants stated, one transformation worked through with its tense rules, and the verification test that closes the method.

questions.prompt: Attempt seven of eight rather than all eight. Is this the right strategy? Discuss.
questions.answer: The arithmetic of the instruction makes a case for selectivity. Where every wrong attempt cancels a right one, the expected value of attempting an uncertain item is close to zero, and if guessing is worse than even, negative: an item attempted in doubt can reduce the total while an item left alone costs nothing. Against that, the seventh and eighth items are chosen by the examiner to be attemptable — the paper is not designed so that a well-prepared student must leave two blanks — and a student who routinely skips two may be skipping the two that his preparation could actually have handled, which converts caution into lost marks. The case therefore depends on what attempt means in practice. For a student whose accuracy on practised items is high, the rational rule is to attempt every item on which a decision can be reached from the grammar itself, and to guess only where two options have already been eliminated — at which point the arithmetic favours attempting, since a one-in-two chance beats leaving the mark unclaimed. For a student still acquiring tense and clause control, attempting all eight simply adds noise, because his errors will not be the random errors of guessing but the systematic errors of a rule applied wrongly, which do cancel correct answers. The strategy must also be weighed against the section’s size: 7 of 80 marks cannot justify extended deliberation, so the practical rule is to answer the seven that yield quickly, mark the eighth, and return only if time permits elsewhere. The strongest answer therefore rejects the question’s framing — the instruction is not a strategic choice to be optimised once but a pacing device that changes with preparedness — and states the decision rule the student should actually follow: attempt everything you can decide, guess after elimination, and never spend literature-section time on a grammar blank.
questions.explanation: Full marks require the expected-value argument, the counter-argument about systematic versus random error, and a decision rule tied to preparedness and to the section’s marks.
